question: Why do practical influence-function estimates disagree with leave-one-out retraining in neural networks, and is there a different, precisely defined response function that they approximate well?

key_findings.claim: The paper decomposes influence-versus-LOO disagreement into three estimand gaps and two approximation errors.
key_findings.evidence: The sequential path separates (1) cold-start from warm-start retraining, (2) warm-start retraining from a damping-induced parameter-proximal objective, (3) continued optimization from a response anchored to the current model's predictions, (4) nonlinear from locally linearized response, and (5) exact from iterative inverse-Hessian-vector solution. The first three are called gaps because they change the question; the last two approximate a fixed surrogate.

key_findings.claim: The Proximal Bregman Response Function (PBRF) formalizes the local, model-preserving question that damped practical influence functions more naturally answer.
key_findings.evidence: PBRF minimizes Bregman divergence from the current model's training predictions, subtracts the loss of the downweighted example, and adds an L2 penalty around the current parameters. Linearizing model outputs and the loss yields a Gauss-Newton system whose optimum equals the corresponding damped influence estimate; for non-converged linear models, the response derivative is shown directly. Thus the equivalence is to a damping- and model-dependent surrogate, not to cold-start deletion.

anchors.section: Appendix B.3, PBRF derivation and linear-model condition

key_findings.claim: Across the tested nonlinear models, warm-start, proximity, and non-convergence gaps are usually much larger than linearization and LiSSA solver errors.
key_findings.evidence: The study covers MLP regression/classification, an eight-layer autoencoder, LeNet, AlexNet, VGG13, ResNet-20, and a two-layer Transformer, plus strongly convex logistic regression as a sanity check. For the Transformer on Penn Treebank, reported output-space magnitudes are 57.926, 30.756, and 61.675 for the first three gaps versus 5.002 and 3.316 for linearization and solver error. Logistic regression gaps and errors are near zero.

key_findings.claim: Influence estimates correlate far better with PBRF-induced test-loss changes than with cold- or warm-start deletion in the reported MNIST experiments.
key_findings.evidence: PBRF Pearson correlations are 0.93 for LeNet, 0.98 for MLP, 0.99 for AlexNet, 0.98 for VGG13, and 0.81 for ResNet-20; cold-start correlations range from -0.55 to 0.45 and warm-start correlations from -0.28 to 0.51. Spearman correlation is also strong for most PBRF cases but only 0.52 for LeNet, so agreement is not uniformly near-perfect.

anchors.section: Appendix Tables 6-7, Hessian versus GNH correlations

key_findings.claim: Ablations support the decomposition's qualitative predictions, but the component magnitudes are path-dependent diagnostic distances rather than unique causal shares of total error.
key_findings.evidence: Greater width reduces linearization error, more training reduces non-convergence gap, weight decay generally reduces disagreement, stronger damping reduces solver/linearization error while increasing proximity gap, and removing more data increases warm-start and linearization effects. Each component is the L2 distance between successive objectives in one chosen order; the distances neither sum algebraically to the endpoint discrepancy nor establish that another ordering would assign the same magnitudes.

key_findings.claim: PBRF and influence scores can identify corrupted labels in one small MNIST study, but broader claimed use cases remain unvalidated here.
key_findings.evidence: With 10% of MNIST and 10% randomly corrupted labels, inspecting the 20% of training examples with highest PBRF self-influence finds over 80% of mislabeled examples; influence scores behave similarly and beat random inspection. The paper asserts relevance to poisoning and other influence applications, but the full text experimentally tests only this label-cleaning task beyond response matching.

method.core_idea: Turn a vague failure of influence functions into a sequence of explicit counterfactual objectives, then identify the endpoint surrogate whose local linearization matches the practical damped influence computation.
method.mechanism: Train a base model, delete selected examples under cold-start, warm-start, parameter-proximal, PBRF, and linearized-PBRF objectives, compute influence with LiSSA and a Gauss-Newton Hessian, and measure output-space distances between successive solutions. Correlate their test-loss changes and ablate architecture, optimization, regularization, damping, and deletion size.
assumptions: The loss is convex in model outputs so its Bregman divergence is nonnegative.
Damping makes the local Gauss-Newton system invertible and defines a meaningful proximity preference.
The current model's predictions are an appropriate anchor for separating deletion effects from continued training.
Finite-step optimization of each surrogate is close enough to its intended response function for diagnostic comparison.
Output L2 distance and test-loss correlation capture the aspects of influence relevant to downstream use.
The selected sequential ordering of objectives is informative even though component magnitudes are not order-invariant.

techniques.role: Separates changed estimands from local approximation and numerical-solver error.
Defines deletion response while preserving the current model's predictions and parameters.
Produces a positive-semidefinite local curvature system matching practical influence computation.
Approximates the damped inverse-curvature product without forming the Hessian.
Measures every transition in the chosen chain of response objectives.
Subtracts the effect of training longer using two retraining runs as an alternative local-deletion proxy.

evaluations.setting: Logistic regression, MLPs, autoencoder, four CNN families, and a small Transformer across UCI, MNIST/FashionMNIST, CIFAR-10, and Penn Treebank.
evaluations.metric: Mean L2 distance between paired model outputs on training inputs for each successive gap/error.
evaluations.result: The first three question-changing gaps dominate in most neural networks; linearization and LiSSA errors are much smaller, while strongly convex logistic regression shows almost no discrepancy.
evaluations.baseline: Cold-start and warm-start LOO retraining, proximal retraining, exact/optimized PBRF, and linearized PBRF.

evaluations.setting: Twenty randomly deleted MNIST training examples for MLP, LeNet, AlexNet, VGG13, and ResNet-20.
evaluations.metric: Pearson and Spearman correlation of predicted test-loss changes with influence estimates.
evaluations.result: PBRF correlations are consistently higher than cold- or warm-start retraining, with Pearson 0.81-0.99 across architectures.
evaluations.baseline: Cold-start LOO and warm-start LOO test-loss changes.

evaluations.setting: Two-hidden-layer MNIST MLP under width, depth, epoch, weight-decay, damping, and deletion-fraction sweeps.
evaluations.metric: Magnitude of each of the five sequential discrepancy terms.
evaluations.result: Observed trends mostly match the proposed mechanisms, including reduced non-convergence with training and a damping tradeoff between conditioning and proximity bias.

evaluations.metric: Fraction of mislabeled points recovered versus fraction of training data manually inspected.
evaluations.result: PBRF self-influence recovers more than 80% of corrupted labels after inspecting 20% of examples; approximate influence is similar and both beat random ranking.

evaluations.setting: Regression/classification comparison using Hessian rather than Gauss-Newton influence and a two-stage LOO alternative.
evaluations.result: PBRF remains more correlated with influence than retraining; two-stage LOO improves over warm-start LOO but remains below PBRF.
evaluations.baseline: GNH-based influence, ordinary warm-start LOO, and PBRF.

limitations: PBRF is a constructed surrogate that depends on current predictions, damping, parameterization, and the chosen loss; matching it does not recover the actual cold-start deletion counterfactual.
The five reported magnitudes are distances along one sequential path, not signed or order-invariant causal contributions to the endpoint mismatch.
Most deletion experiments use only 20 random training examples, limiting uncertainty and tail-behavior analysis.
Several vision experiments use only 10% of MNIST, and the language model is a two-layer, two-head Transformer trained for ten epochs on Penn Treebank.
Cold-start retraining reuses the original initialization and batch order, which controls noise but understates the distribution of retraining outcomes across seeds.
Proximal objectives are optimized for half the base training epochs and may have objective-specific optimization error that is not isolated.
LiSSA scaling is tuned over a broad grid and other solvers, curvature approximations, stochastic batches, and stopping rules may alter conclusions.
Output-space L2 distance can be insensitive to application-specific behavior and is not equivalent to ranking quality or causal data value.
Only mislabeled-example discovery is demonstrated as a downstream PBRF use case; poisoning, fairness, augmentation, and explanation claims are asserted rather than tested.
The study predates current billion-parameter LLM attribution regimes, where curvature approximation, convergence, and behavior-level evaluation are more severe.
failure_modes: PBRF faithfully matches influence estimates that are themselves irrelevant to the user's desired cold-start or seed-averaged counterfactual.
A large damping value makes the system numerically stable while answering an overly local parameter-space question.
Different parameterizations represent the same function but yield different proximity penalties and influence rankings.
LiSSA appears accurate on average but fails for rare high-curvature examples or insufficient batch sizes.
The current model has memorized corrupted labels, so preserving its predictions conflicts with identifying harmful data.
Sequential gap magnitudes change when the audit order changes, leading readers to mistake a diagnostic path for a unique decomposition.
High correlation with PBRF conceals poor top-k ranking, sign errors, or downstream deletion effects.
Scaling to large removal groups leaves the local regime and sharply increases linearization error.
reusable_insights: Name the counterfactual estimand before evaluating an attribution approximation; cold-start deletion, local warm-start response, and behavior preservation are different questions.
Separate estimand shift from numerical approximation error rather than treating all disagreement as one solver failure.
Use a tractable exact or optimization-based surrogate such as PBRF to tune inverse-curvature solvers, then independently validate the surrogate on the intended downstream task.
Report ranking, sign, top-k recovery, output change, and downstream utility alongside correlation.
Audit damping as a semantic choice, not merely a numerical stabilizer, because it defines the strength of parameter proximity.
When a base model is not converged, control for continued-training effects before interpreting deletion response.
Treat decomposition order as an experimental factor and test whether conclusions survive alternative paths.
open_questions: Which data-attribution tasks genuinely want a PBRF-style local behavior-preserving estimand rather than seed-averaged retraining?
Can proximity be defined in function space alone to reduce parameterization dependence?
How stable are PBRF and influence rankings across model seeds, checkpoints, damping choices, and label noise?
Can the five-way diagnostic be made order-invariant or replaced by a factorial intervention analysis?
What solver and curvature approximation best predict PBRF at billion-parameter scale under a fixed compute budget?
Does strong PBRF agreement predict successful data removal, unlearning, poisoning detection, fairness repair, or compensation decisions?
How should influence be evaluated when model behavior changes discontinuously after retraining or when multiple equivalent optima exist?
Can scalable retraining ensembles provide a better target than either one LOO run or a locally constructed surrogate?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Koh and Liang operationalize classical influence with Hessian-vector products and evaluate neural-network debugging, errors, and poisoning against deletion intuition; the reviewed paper dissects why that deletion interpretation fails and proposes PBRF as the local target.

competitive_landscape.title: Influence Functions in Deep Learning Are Fragile
competitive_landscape.difference: Basu et al. show influence accuracy depends strongly on depth, width, regularization, and test points when judged against LOO; the reviewed work accepts the mismatch but attributes most of it to a different estimand rather than fragile local approximation.

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Up Influence Functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Schioppa et al. use Arnoldi iteration to scale influence to large vision and language Transformers; the reviewed paper focuses on defining the target and uses LiSSA, so the works address computational versus semantic sources of error.

competitive_landscape.title: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
competitive_landscape.difference: TRAK uses random projections and an after-kernel across a handful of trained models to approximate attribution methods otherwise requiring thousands of retrains; it targets scalable empirical attribution rather than explaining practical influence as PBRF.

competitive_landscape.title: Revisiting inverse Hessian vector products for calculating influence functions
competitive_landscape.difference: Klochkov and Liu derive LiSSA hyperparameter requirements from Hessian spectral properties and explicitly validate against PBRF, extending the reviewed paper's surrogate target with a more systematic numerical analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Do Influence Functions Work on Large Language Models?
competitive_landscape.difference: Li et al. report consistently poor influence performance on LLM tasks and attribute it to inverse-curvature error, uncertain convergence, and parameter changes failing to track behavior; this tests a scale and behavioral regime far beyond the reviewed paper's two-layer Transformer and tempers its optimistic conclusion.

novelty_assessment: The central conceptual move is strong: it distinguishes failures caused by approximating a fixed response from disagreements caused by silently changing the counterfactual question, and it supplies PBRF as an optimizable target for the local question. The empirical breadth across small model families is useful. The result does not rehabilitate influence functions as approximations to real retraining, and PBRF should not be promoted as a universal gold standard without task-level validation, seed robustness, and parameterization audits. Later solver work adopts PBRF, while LLM-scale studies show that both computation and behavioral relevance remain open.
reviewer_notes: Read all 28 cached pages, including the five objectives and derivations, complete model/dataset results, all ablations, exact optimization and LiSSA protocols, numerical tables with and without Gauss-Newton curvature, two-stage LOO, and mislabeled-MNIST experiment. Six primary proceedings/arXiv competitors and later stress tests were checked on 2026-08-23. Scope audit: the paper establishes close agreement with a deliberately local PBRF surrogate on modest models, not accurate cold-start deletion or large-model data attribution. Contradiction audit: calling PBRF an alternative gold standard is justified for solver debugging but not for every application; only one downstream label-cleaning experiment is shown, and the sequential gap magnitudes are order-dependent distances rather than a unique causal decomposition.
